idiom_name: servlet Filter with a JCache (JSR-107) or Caffeine store
implementation_notes: The classic JVM realization is a javax.servlet/jakarta.servlet Filter that wraps the response in a caching wrapper: on a hit it copies the stored headers and bytes back and never calls chain.doFilter(); on a miss it captures the rendered bytes, stores them in a JCache (JSR-107) provider or Caffeine under a key built from method + request URI + the Vary axes, and lets the response through. The container supplies the interception point (URL mapping, filter order, encoding), so the hand-written lookup layer other languages need is replaced by configuration, while TTL and eviction policy come from the cache provider. It remains the right shape for servlet-based, anonymous, expensive pages; when an MVC framework renders the page, caching the render step instead (see the spring-cacheable-render variant) keeps the response out of the wrapper's reach.
pitfalls: A response wrapper must buffer without flushing: HttpServletResponse commits headers early, so a wrapper that leaks a flush breaks sendRedirect/error handling downstream, and it must never be applied to authenticated or cookie-setting endpoints.
JCache and Caffeine stores are per-JVM, so in a cluster every node caches privately: purge means a shared provider (Redis, memcached, Hazelcast) or accepting per-node staleness with short TTLs.
Caching filters interact badly with frameworks that stream output or read the request body themselves; scope the filter by URL pattern to the static-ish pages it is meant to serve.

variants.name: Servlet filter page cache over JCache/Caffeine
Spring @Cacheable on the rendering service (+ ShallowEtagHeaderFilter)
variants.idiom_name: @Cacheable("pages") on the page-assembly method, backed by a CacheManager
variants.implementation_notes: If a Spring MVC controller produces a rendered body, the cache belongs one level down at the rendering service: annotate the pure method that assembles the page with @Cacheable(cacheNames = "pages", key = ...), back it with a CacheManager (Caffeine in-process, Redis for a shared cache) and let Spring's proxy return the stored value, while the freshness metadata is declared separately - CacheControl/max-age on the response or a ShallowEtagHeaderFilter for conditional GETs. This keeps caching out of the controller (annotation-on-controller is a known misuse), gives declarative eviction via @CacheEvict, and per the framework docs has been the API since Spring 3.1; the floor recorded here is the current Spring Boot 3 / Spring Framework 6 baseline of Java 17.
pitfalls: Self-invocation bypasses the proxy: calling renderArticlePage(...) from another method of the same bean renders on every request, with no error and no cache hit.
Keys built only from method arguments leak personalisation - anything the method reads from the SecurityContext, RequestContextHolder or a ThreadLocal must be part of the SpEL key.
@Cacheable hands the same instance to every caller: the returned value must be immutable, or one caller's mutation is served to all of them.
